# Ono & Ikegami autopoietic protocells

`ono-ikegami-protocell` · *Ono & Ikegami, 1999-2003*

## Introduction

Ono and Ikegami's protocell model asks how a cell could hold itself together
before there were genes. A living cell is a bag of chemistry, and the bag is
made by the chemistry it contains: reactions inside produce the membrane, and
the membrane keeps those reactions from drifting apart. Naoaki Ono and Takashi
Ikegami, at the University of Tokyo, built a series of spatial artificial
chemistries to show that this loop can arise on its own. A simple metabolism
makes membrane particles, the membrane particles gather into walls because
they avoid water, and the walls enclose the metabolism that made them. In some
regimes the enclosed structure grows and splits in two.

The picture is a grid of particles of five kinds. *Autocatalysts* copy
themselves out of food, and also turn food into membrane particles. Membrane
particles are *hydrophobic*: water and autocatalysts push them away, as water
pushes oil away. Food and waste are neutral and only weakly pushed. Everything
except water decays into waste, and an outside energy source turns waste back
into food. If membrane surrounds a patch rich in autocatalyst, the patch keeps
replacing the membrane as it decays, while food still seeps in. That is a
*protocell*: a self-maintaining compartment with no genome.

The idea comes from *autopoiesis* ("self-production"). Ono and Ikegami (2000)
cite Maturana and Varela (1980), who "stressed that self-maintenance of this
boundary is an indispensable feature for living cells". Their journal paper of
2000 works the idea out in one dimension, where two walls are enough to trap a
cell. The two-dimensional version the book describes (Ono and Ikegami 1999,
2001) adds one ingredient: membrane particles can be *anisotropic*, repelling
more strongly in one direction than in the others. The book reports that this
is crucial for protocells to form, above all when food is scarce. Later work
took the model to three dimensions.

It is a simulation model. Banzhaf and Yamamoto place it at the end of their
origin-of-life chapter (book §6.3.2, "Emergence of Protocells with ACs").
Its closest neighbour in the catalog is
[the Varela–Maturana–Uribe autopoiesis model](autopoiesis-vmu.md), where a
catalyst makes links that bond into a chain by explicit rules. Here nothing
bonds: the membrane holds together only because its particles avoid water,
and many autocatalysts share the space. [The chemoton](chemoton.md) couples
metabolism, template and membrane by fixed stoichiometry in a well-mixed
cell, and [GARD](gard.md) models well-mixed lipid assemblies without space.
[NAC](nac.md) also demixes hydrophilic and hydrophobic particles, but on a
graph and with no metabolism. As the book says, this model has no genetic
material and no evolution.

Chemart's implementation is partial. The papers that define the
two-dimensional model could not be obtained, so the lattice rules are
reconstructed from the book and the one-dimensional paper. The reconstruction
reproduces membrane particles separating from water, and the contrast between
isotropic and anisotropic membrane, but not the closed, dividing protocells
that are the model's main published result.

| **network** | given — the chemistry is a reaction network, instantiated from its parameters |

## How it works

### Particles on a hexagonal grid

The world is a hexagonal lattice wrapped into a torus (its edges join, so
there is no boundary), with exactly one particle in every cell. Each cell has
six neighbours, 60 degrees apart. The five species are:

| species | stands for | behaves |
|---|---|---|
| `A` | autocatalyst | hydrophilic (water-like) |
| `M` | membrane particle | hydrophobic; isotropic `M_i` or anisotropic `M_a` |
| `X` | food | neutral |
| `Y` | waste | neutral |
| `W` | water | hydrophilic |

A reaction changes what one particle *is*; motion swaps two neighbours.

### The reactions

The book's scheme:

```
A + X -> 2 A           an autocatalyst turns neighbouring food into another A
A + X -> A + M         ... or into membrane; A is unchanged (a catalyst)
A -> Y, M -> Y, X -> Y everything except water decays to waste
Y -> X                 the external energy source recycles waste into food
```

Once per sweep every cell is updated at the same time. A food particle with
`n` autocatalysts among its six neighbours becomes `A` with probability
`P_A × n`, becomes `M` with probability `P_M × n`, and otherwise decays with
probability `P_decay`. `A` and `M` decay with probability `P_decay`, and
waste becomes food with probability `X_supply`, the food supply. Water never
reacts.

### Why membrane particles gather

Every pair of neighbours has an energy. A hydrophilic particle (`A` or `W`)
next to a membrane particle costs `repulsion`; a neutral one (`X` or `Y`)
costs only `neutral_coupling × repulsion`; every other pair costs nothing.
Membrane particles do not attract each other. They end up together because
each membrane–water contact they remove lowers the energy.

Particles move by swapping places with a neighbour (a *Kawasaki exchange*,
which keeps every cell full). A swap is judged by the *Metropolis rule*: if it
lowers the energy it is accepted; if it raises it by ΔE it is accepted with
probability exp(−ΔE/T), where T is the `temperature`. Downhill swaps win on
average, and noise lets the system escape poor arrangements. Because food and
waste are only weakly repelled, they can slip past a wall that holds back the
strongly repelled autocatalyst: that is the intended selective permeability.

### Isotropic and anisotropic membrane

An isotropic `M_i` repels equally in all six directions. The book's figure
6.13 shows that an anisotropic `M_a` repels more strongly in one direction,
but gives no formula, so Chemart chose one. Each `M_a` carries an orientation
`o`, one of the six directions, and its repulsion toward direction `k` is
scaled by

```
F[k, o] = 1 + a·cos(2 × 60° × (k − o))
```

where `a` is the `anisotropy`. The average over the six directions is 1, so
`M_a` carries the same total repulsion as `M_i`, only distributed
differently. At the default `a = 2.4`, `anisotropy_field(2.4, False)` gives,
for an `M_a` pointing in direction 0:

```
direction k:  0     1     2     3     4     5
F[k, 0]:      3.4  -0.2  -0.2   3.4  -0.2  -0.2
```

Water at either end (directions 0 and 3) costs 3.4 times the basic repulsion;
water on the four flanks is slightly *favourable*. An `M_a` therefore wants
membrane neighbours at its two ends and water along its sides, and a line of
them end to end is a wall one particle thick. An `M_i` simply minimises its
water contact, which a compact blob does best. That is the difference between
a membrane and an oil droplet. Each sweep, every `M_a` also proposes a random
new orientation, accepted by the same Metropolis rule.

### One sweep

A run is `steps` sweeps. Each sweep does `relaxation` exchange passes (each
picks one direction and tries to swap non-overlapping neighbour pairs along
it; swaps involving `A` are tried only with probability 1/`mobility_ratio`),
then one rotation pass for `M_a`, then one chemistry pass. A new `M_a` gets a
random orientation. Many exchange passes per chemistry pass let particles sort
themselves before they react, standing in for the one-dimensional paper, where
particles move with probability 7×10⁻³ per step and reaction probabilities
are of order 10⁻⁴ or less.

### A worked example: the default run

The default run starts from a well-mixed 24×24 lattice (576 cells): 48
autocatalysts, 178 food particles, 350 water, no membrane. After 100 sweeps
it holds 100 `A`, 99 `M_a`, 20 `X`, 7 `Y` and still 350 `W`. The reaction
counts show how it got there:

```
A + X -> 2 A  (x158)
A + X -> A + M_a  (x160)
A -> Y  (x106)
M_a -> Y  (x61)
X -> Y  (x46)
Y -> X  (x206)
```

The autocatalyst population roughly doubled: 158 replications against 106
decays, 48 + 158 − 106 = 100. It made 160 membrane particles, of which 61
decayed, leaving 99. Every decay produced waste, and 206 waste particles were
recycled into food. Food is now scarce (20 left), which limits further growth.
The membrane lies in 43 separate pieces, the largest of 10 particles, and a
membrane particle has on average 1.45 membrane neighbours: short, thin
fragments, not blobs. No enclosed compartment has formed.

### Formal specification

Banzhaf and Yamamoto describe every artificial chemistry by three things (book §2.3): the set of possible molecules **S**, the reaction rules **R** that transform them, and the reactor algorithm **A** that decides which reactions happen, and when. For this chemistry:

**S — molecules** (*explicit* — listed up front). five species A (autocatalyst, hydrophilic), M (membrane, hydrophobic, isotropic M_i or anisotropic M_a carrying one of the six lattice orientations), X (food, neutral), Y (waste, neutral), W (water, hydrophilic), one particle per cell of a hexagonal torus

**R — reactions** (*explicit* — listed reaction by reaction; molecules per reaction: 1, 2). A + X -&gt; 2 A ; A + X -&gt; A + M ; A -&gt; Y, M -&gt; Y, X -&gt; Y (decay) ; Y -&gt; X (recycling by an external energy source)

plus hydrophobic/hydrophilic repulsion; an anisotropic M_a spreads the same total repulsion unevenly over the six directions, which is what turns membrane clusters into filaments

**A — reactor**: `lattice-2d` (a two-dimensional grid on which only neighbours interact).

*How the population is bounded:* none: the lattice is closed and every cell holds exactly one particle; the external energy source enters as the recycling reaction Y -&gt; X, whose rate X_supply is the food supply

Kawasaki exchange with a neighbour plus rotation of M_a, both accepted with the Metropolis rule min(1, exp(-dE/T)); the reactions are then applied cell by cell

### Using it in Chemart

Every parameter at its default:

```python
import chemart
net = chemart.generate_network("ono-ikegami-protocell", seed=1)
print(net.summary())
```

```
ono-ikegami-protocell: 5 species, 6 reactions, status=observed
provides: catalysts, energies, initial-state, space, stoichiometry, topology
seed: 1
extras: analysis, energies, space
```

Its first reactions (`net.reactions`):

```
A + X -> 2 A  (x158)
A + X -> A + M_a  (x160)
A -> Y  (x106)
M_a -> Y  (x61)
X -> Y  (x46)
Y -> X  (x206)
```

The default run (about two seconds) is not a published experiment: the
published parameters belong to a different reaction scheme (see Results), so
the defaults were chosen to be small and fast. `mode="reactions"` returns just the six
reactions of the scheme, each with `rate` set to `None`, since no source
publishes a rate for it.

What a spatial run leaves in `net.extras`:

- `space["final"]`: the lattice as rows of `A`, `M`, `X`, `Y`, `W`, and
  `space["orientations"]` the direction (0–5) of each membrane particle. Rows
  are in axial hexagonal coordinates, so printed as a square grid the picture
  is sheared.
- `analysis["counts"]` and `analysis["history"]`: the species counts at the
  end and after every sweep.
- The membrane's shape: `membrane_clusters`, `largest_membrane_cluster`,
  `mean_membrane_coordination` (membrane neighbours per membrane particle,
  about 5 inside a blob and about 2 along a thin filament) and
  `membrane_alignment` (the fraction of membrane contacts that run along both
  particles' axes; 1/9 for random orientations).
- Compartments: `protocells` counts regions of non-membrane cells enclosed by
  membrane, with sizes and contents in `protocell_details`, and `enclosed_A`
  totals the autocatalysts inside. A single water cell boxed in by membrane
  counts, so check the sizes.
- `energies["reference_rates"]`: the one-dimensional paper's constants, kept
  for reference and not used by the simulation.

### Droplets versus filaments

The contrast of the book's figure 6.14, with chemistry switched off so that
only self-assembly acts: 12% scattered membrane particles and strong
repulsion.

```python
import chemart
NOCHEM = dict(P_A=0.0, P_M=0.0, P_decay=0.0, X_supply=0.0)
for seed in (1, 2):
    for membrane in ("anisotropic", "isotropic"):
        a = chemart.generate_network(
            "ono-ikegami-protocell", seed=seed, membrane=membrane,
            repulsion=5.0, relaxation=25, steps=60,
            M_fraction=0.12, A_fraction=0.0, X_fraction=0.20, **NOCHEM,
        ).extras["analysis"]
        print(seed, membrane, a["mean_membrane_coordination"],
              a["membrane_alignment"], a["largest_membrane_cluster"],
              a["membrane_clusters"])
```

```
1 anisotropic 1.28 0.4583 19 34
1 isotropic 4.6667 0.0971 48 3
2 anisotropic 1.7143 0.4833 11 20
2 isotropic 4.6286 0.1173 66 5
```

Isotropic particles collapse into a few compact blobs (for seed 1, pieces of
48 and 26 of the 75 particles) with about 4.7 membrane neighbours each.
Anisotropic particles stay thin (1.3 to 1.7 neighbours) and line up along
their axes (46–48% of contacts, against 11% at random), but in 20 to 34
short pieces rather than closed walls. Each run takes one to three seconds.

### A cell, fed and starved

`initial="cell"` places a membrane ring of radius `cell_radius` around a mix
of autocatalyst and food, a two-dimensional version of the one-dimensional
paper's cell experiment. Switching the food supply off shows the metabolism
depending on the energy source:

```python
for supply in (0.30, 0.0):
    a = chemart.generate_network(
        "ono-ikegami-protocell", seed=1, X_supply=supply,
        repulsion=5.0, relaxation=20, steps=100,
        initial="cell", cell_radius=5, width=24, height=24,
    ).extras["analysis"]
    h = a["history"]["A"]
    print(supply, a["counts"], h[0], max(h), h[-1], a["protocells"])
```

```
0.3 {'A': 96, 'M': 111, 'X': 37, 'Y': 5, 'W': 327} 31 96 96 0
0.0 {'A': 48, 'M': 41, 'X': 1, 'Y': 159, 'W': 327} 31 83 48 0
```

Fed, the autocatalyst grows from 31 to 96. Starved, food runs out, waste piles
up and the autocatalyst falls from a peak of 83 to 48. In both runs the ring
itself is gone: already after one sweep no compartment is left and the
largest membrane piece has 7 particles. Each run takes under two seconds.

`mobility_ratio` slows the autocatalyst, as in the one-dimensional paper's
dividing cells (which used 5), and `anisotropy=0` makes `M_a` behave like
`M_i`. The lattice goes up to 200×200; cost grows with cells × `steps` ×
`relaxation`, and 100×100 for 200 sweeps at the defaults takes about seven
seconds.

#### Parameters

Pass any of these as keyword arguments to `generate_network`. The *role* column says what a parameter controls: `structural` (which molecules and reactions exist), `kinetic` (rates), `thermodynamic` (energies, temperature), `population` (sizes, budgets, initial state), `spatial`, `stochastic` or `selection`. *range* gives the values used in the published work.

| name | type | default | role | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mode` | `enum` | `spatial` | structural | 'reactions' returns the four-reaction network on its own; 'spatial' runs the lattice and returns the reactions that fired with their counts, plus the lattice, the energies and the protocell measurements <br>one of `spatial`, `reactions` |
| `membrane` | `enum` | `anisotropic` | structural | whether membrane particles are the anisotropic M_a or the isotropic M_i; the book's central result is that only M_a sustains protocells at low food supply <br>one of `anisotropic`, `isotropic` |
| `width` | `int` | `24` | spatial | lattice width in cells (axial r); the papers use a few hundred <br>`6` … `200` |
| `height` | `int` | `24` | spatial | lattice height in cells (axial q) <br>`6` … `200` |
| `steps` | `int` | `100` | population | lattice sweeps; each sweep does six Metropolis exchange passes, one rotation pass and one chemistry pass <br>`1` … `20000` |
| `relaxation` | `int` | `12` | spatial | Metropolis exchange passes per chemistry pass; this is where the paper's separation between the mobility rates (7e-3) and the reaction rates (1e-4) enters, so particles demix long before they react <br>`1` … `200` |
| `initial` | `enum` | `random` | population | 'random' is a well-mixed start (the papers' homogeneous experiment); 'cell' prepares a membrane ring around autocatalyst and food (their cell-like experiment) <br>one of `random`, `cell` |
| `cell_radius` | `int` | `5` | spatial | radius in cells of the prepared membrane ring when initial = cell <br>`1` … `60` |
| `A_fraction` | `float` | `0.08` | population | fraction of cells seeded with autocatalyst A when initial = random <br>`0` … `1` |
| `X_fraction` | `float` | `0.3` | population | fraction of cells seeded with food X; the rest of the lattice is water W <br>`0` … `1` |
| `M_fraction` | `float` | `0.0` | population | fraction of cells seeded with membrane M when initial = random; non-zero starts from dispersed membrane particles, so their self-assembly can be watched on its own <br>`0` … `1` |
| `P_A` | `float` | `0.03` | kinetic | probability per sweep and per neighbouring A that a food particle replicates it (A + X -&gt; 2 A); the paper's reproduction rate of A <br>`0` … `1` |
| `P_M` | `float` | `0.03` | kinetic | probability per sweep and per neighbouring A that a food particle becomes membrane (A + X -&gt; A + M); the paper's production rate of M <br>`0` … `1` |
| `P_decay` | `float` | `0.01` | kinetic | probability per sweep that an A, M or X particle decays to waste Y; water never decays <br>`0` … `1` |
| `X_supply` | `float` | `0.3` | kinetic | probability per sweep that waste is recycled to food (Y -&gt; X) by the external energy source; the decisive resource-supply parameter, low values being the regime where anisotropy pays off <br>`0` … `1` |
| `anisotropy` | `float` | `2.4` | spatial | strength a of the directional part of the M_a repulsion field, F[k, o] = 1 + a cos(2 * 60deg * (k - o)): repulsion is strongest along the +-o axis and weakest on the four flanks, where it turns attractive once a &gt; 2, so a membrane particle wants membrane neighbours along its axis and water on both flanks; 0 makes M_a behave like M_i <br>`0` … `3` |
| `repulsion` | `float` | `1.0` | thermodynamic | energy of one hydrophilic/hydrophobic neighbour pair, in units of the temperature <br>≥ `0` |
| `neutral_coupling` | `float` | `0.25` | thermodynamic | energy of a neutral/hydrophobic pair as a fraction of `repulsion`; this weak coupling is what lets X and Y cross a membrane that holds A back <br>`0` … `1` |
| `temperature` | `float` | `1.0` | thermodynamic | Metropolis temperature T in min(1, exp(-dE/T)) <br>≥ `0.01` |
| `mobility_ratio` | `float` | `1.0` | spatial | the paper's m: exchanges involving A are attempted with probability 1/m, making the autocatalyst less mobile than membrane and food; the 1D paper needs m = 5 for a cell to divide <br>≥ `1` |

### Implementation decisions

The sources leave gaps, and sometimes contradict each other or the book. Each such case, and how Chemart resolved it, is listed here: read these before quoting a number from this page.

??? note "9 decisions"

    - The book describes the two-dimensional hexagonal model of [639]/[641]; those papers, the BioSystems study [637] and the 3D extension [538] are all paywalled and were not obtainable (no open copy per OpenAlex/Unpaywall/Semantic Scholar, and the Internet Archive was offline during this work). The accessible primary source is the authors' 1D predecessor, Ono & Ikegami (2000), whose appendix A supplies the lattice algorithm reconstructed here.
    - That 1D model runs a different reaction scheme - it inserts an enzyme E (A + A -&gt; A + E, E + R -&gt; E + A, E + R -&gt; E + M) and its resource/waste are R and W, whereas the book's 2D model has A act directly and names the five species A, M, X, Y, W. The implemented reaction set is the book's; the 1D constants (P_E = 0.5e-6, P_A' = 2e-6, P_R = P_W = 100e-6, P_D = 7e-3, P_R0 = 5e-3, P_R1 = 0.5 P_R0, m = 1 or 5) therefore do NOT apply to it and are recorded, with the phase-diagram points of figures 4, 7 and 10, in extras.reference_rates rather than used as rate constants.
    - Consequently every reaction carries rate = None: no accessible source publishes a rate for this scheme. P_A, P_M, P_decay and X_supply are simulation probabilities per sweep whose defaults were chosen so the zero-argument run is small and fast, and are not published values.
    - Ono & Ikegami coarse-grain space into sites holding 100 particles each. Here each cell of the hexagonal torus holds exactly one particle, which is what lets M_a carry the orientation the book's figure 6.13 requires, and particles move by Kawasaki exchange under the Metropolis rule instead of the paper's probability-proportional hopping. Both conserve the occupancy of every cell, which is the property the paper's swap rule exists to enforce.
    - The anisotropic field is nematic, F[k, o] = 1 + a cos(2 * 60deg * (k - o)), with mean 1 over the six directions, so M_i and M_a carry the same total repulsion and differ only in how it is distributed: strongest along the +-o axis, weakest on the four flanks. The book's figure 6.13 shows a darker (more repulsive) direction around M_a and gives no formula; the 180-degree-symmetric form was chosen because a membrane has two equivalent sides. The default a = 2.4 is past the point where the flank term goes negative, which is what distinguishes a membrane from a droplet: a purely repulsive M_i minimises its water contact and collapses into a compact blob, whereas an amphiphilic M_a wants membrane neighbours along its axis and water on both flanks, giving the one-particle-thick filaments the book describes.
    - Equation (A.8) of the 2000 paper appears to divide the membrane mobility by m as well, which contradicts its own section 3.3 and the caption of figure 10 ('A and E particles have lower diffusion and repulsion rates than M and R'). The prose is followed: mobility_ratio slows only A.
    - Equations (B.1) and (B.2) write the spontaneous resource-to-autocatalyst term as P_A' W_0 although (A.2) makes it proportional to the local resource; that term is not part of the book's scheme, so the discrepancy is recorded but not implemented.
    - What this implementation does and does not reproduce. Reproduced and tested: membrane particles demix from water; isotropic M_i collapses into compact droplets while anisotropic M_a builds thin, orientationally ordered filaments (the contrast of figure 6.14); and the metabolism collapses when the recycling of waste into food is switched off. NOT reproduced: filaments closing into protocells, the osmotic permeability of a closed membrane to X and Y while it retains A, and growth followed by division. Prepared membrane rings dissolve rather than persisting, and no enclosed compartment ever retained autocatalyst. Those three phenomena are the results of [639]/[641], whose lattice rules were not obtainable, so they are listed in `phenomena` as published claims but are not asserted by the tests.
    - The v1 parameters are replaced: grid becomes width/height, rate_constants becomes the four probabilities above, repulsion_strength becomes repulsion/neutral_coupling/temperature, anisotropy becomes the enum `membrane` plus the strength `anisotropy`, and dimensions is dropped because only the 2D model is implemented ([538]'s 3D lattice was not obtainable). The v1 claims of rate-constants and flow are dropped: no rate is published, and the lattice is closed rather than a flow reactor.

## Results

### One dimension: self-maintenance and two kinds of reproduction

The only primary paper available for this entry, Ono and Ikegami (2000), uses
a different scheme: an autocatalyst `A` turns another `A` into an
enzyme `E`, and `E` makes new `A` and membrane `M` from a resource. Space is a
ring of 100 sites holding 100 particles each, and each phase-diagram run
lasts 1,000,000 iterations. From a uniform start, the final density of
autocatalyst divides the plane of the two production rates, of `A` and of
`M`, into three regions (their figure 5): in region 0 it dies out, in region
II it always becomes dense, and in region I the outcome depends on the
starting density. A mean-field analysis (their appendix B) explains region I
as two stable states created by saddle-node bifurcations. With enough
autocatalyst, membrane particles form "periodic clusters of about 20 sites"
(figure 4).

Starting instead from a cell, a pocket of autocatalyst between two walls,
region I splits into three subregions (figures 7 and 8). In Ia the membrane is not
replaced fast enough and the cell disappears; in Ib the cell keeps a constant
size; in Ic the membrane is thin, autocatalyst leaks out, multiplies and
builds new membranes, until space is filled with cells of a typical size.
The authors call this *open reproduction*, since daughter cells are built
from particles that permeated out rather than from the mother's contents. A
cell larger than its stable size splits by building a wall in its middle
(figure 9). When `A` and `E` diffuse and repel five times more slowly than
the other particles (`m = 5`, figure 10), the cell pushes its walls outward,
reaches a critical size and divides, recursively: *closed reproduction*, in
which the contents stay inside. The paper says this kind "has greater
potential to inherit internal information than the other way of
reproduction."

### Two dimensions: protocells from a random start

According to the book, after preliminary work (Ono and Ikegami 1999), the
2001 paper shows membrane-like clusters of irregular shape forming on the
hexagonal lattice. Some close into cells that let small food particles cross
by osmosis while keeping their metabolism inside, and some grow and divide.
Anisotropic particles are crucial: with isotropic ones only, clusters form
but shrink and disappear because they cannot sustain an internal metabolism.
The advantage is clearest under low food supply (book figure 6.14). Ono
(2005) studied the conditions for protocell emergence in more depth, and
Madina, Ono and Ikegami (2003) moved to three dimensions, finding parallel
membranes joined by tubes, and intertwined filaments that organise into
globular structures. None of these papers could be obtained, so their numbers
are not given here.

### What Chemart reproduces

The tests (`tests/chemistries/test_ono_ikegami_protocell.py`) cover the
catalog's six phenomena as follows.

- **Membrane demixes from water; anisotropic clusters are filaments that
  close into protocells.** Demixing and filaments are reproduced; closing is
  not. The test runs the droplet-versus-filament recipe on two seeds and
  requires `M_a` to have fewer than 2.5 membrane neighbours and more than 30%
  aligned contacts, and `M_i` more than 2.5 neighbours and under 20%.
- **Isotropic clusters die out, anisotropic ones give dividing protocells,
  most clearly at low food supply.** Only the shape contrast is reproduced.
  At `X_supply=0.05` for 300 sweeps, both membrane kinds keep 74 to 94
  autocatalysts on seeds 1–3, and the only compartment (anisotropic, seed 2)
  holds no autocatalyst.
- **A closed membrane lets food and waste through but holds the autocatalyst
  in; a protocell grows and divides.** Not reproduced: no closed membrane
  persists, and the prepared ring dissolves within the first sweep.
- **Without recycling of waste into food the cell starves and collapses.**
  Reproduced by the fed-and-starved recipe. Starved, food ends at most 10,
  waste exceeds three times the fed run's, and the autocatalyst ends below
  its peak and below the fed run.
- **Three dimensions.** Not implemented.

Other tests check the six reactions and the absence of invented rates, the
anisotropy field (mean 1, values 3.4 and −0.2 at `a = 2.4`), and the
one-dimensional paper's constants as recorded; its phase diagrams are not
simulated. The gap comes from the reconstruction: one particle per cell
instead of 100 per site, Metropolis swaps instead of the paper's hopping
probabilities, an anisotropy formula of Chemart's own and unpublished reaction
probabilities (see the implementation decisions above). These rules give
walls and filaments, but not self-maintaining, self-reproducing compartments.

## References

Banzhaf, W. & Yamamoto, L. (2015). *Artificial Chemistries*. MIT Press. Section 6.3.2; the book's bibliography entries [637], [639], [641], [538].

### Sources used for the implementation

- Ono, N. & Ikegami, T. (2000). Self-maintenance and self-reproduction in an abstract cell model. J. theor. Biol. 206:243-253, doi:10.1006/jtbi.2000.2121. Full text from the authors' lab archive, http://sacral.c.u-tokyo.ac.jp/pdf/ono_jtheorbiol_2000.pdf (via the Wayback Machine). Appendix A gives the reaction and mobility rules and every constant; appendix B the mean-field equations; figures 5, 7, 8 and 10 the phase diagram and the parameter values of each regime.
- Banzhaf, W. & Yamamoto, L. (2015). Artificial Chemistries, MIT Press, section 6.3.2 and figures 6.13, 6.14 - the five-species hexagonal model, the isotropic/anisotropic repulsion fields, and the low-supply result.

### Further reading

- Maturana, H. R. & Varela, F. J. (1980). *Autopoiesis and Cognition: the
  Realization of the Living.* Dordrecht: D. Reidel. The source of the
  autopoiesis concept that the model sets out to capture.
- Ono, N. & Ikegami, T. (1999). Model of self-replicating cell capable of
  self-maintenance. In *Proceedings of the Fifth European Conference on
